reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / AASLD
clinicalPearls: Hepatic involvement usually reflects systemic AL (light-chain) amyloidosis, so the liver is rarely affected in isolation and a plasma cell dyscrasia should be sought
Marked hepatomegaly that is out of proportion to only mild liver enzyme changes is a characteristic clue
A disproportionately raised alkaline phosphatase, often with relatively preserved aminotransferases and bilirubin, is a typical biochemical pattern
Coexisting cardiac, renal, or autonomic amyloid and features such as macroglossia or periorbital purpura point toward a systemic process
Diagnosis rests on demonstrating amyloid deposits, classically apple-green birefringence under polarised light after Congo red staining, with typing to confirm the fibril protein
Serum free light-chain assay and serum/urine immunofixation help identify the underlying clonal disorder in AL disease

Percutaneous liver biopsy carries an increased bleeding risk because vascular amyloid infiltration makes the organ friable, so this should be weighed against biopsy of a safer site such as abdominal fat or bone marrow
Treatment is directed at the underlying clone or precursor protein rather than at the liver itself, and outcomes depend heavily on the degree of cardiac involvement
reference.pathophysiology: Amyloidosis results from extracellular deposition of misfolded protein fibrils that adopt a beta-pleated sheet configuration. In hepatic disease the most common type is AL amyloid, in which monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains produced by a plasma cell clone form the fibrils; AA (serum amyloid A) amyloid from chronic inflammation and hereditary transthyretin-related forms can also involve the liver. Fibrils accumulate progressively in the space of Disse and around sinusoids and vessels, compressing hepatocytes and distorting architecture. This produces organomegaly and a predominantly cholestatic biochemical picture, while synthetic function and portal pressure are relatively spared until late; vascular fragility from perivascular deposition underlies the bleeding tendency.
additionalDifferentials: Infiltrative malignancy such as lymphoma or metastatic disease
Congestive hepatopathy from right heart failure
Extrahepatic biliary obstruction causing a cholestatic pattern
additionalInvestigations: Serum free light-chain ratio with serum and urine immunofixation to detect a monoclonal protein
Congo red staining of tissue with confirmatory typing (e.g. mass spectrometry or immunohistochemistry)
Assessment of extrahepatic organ involvement, including cardiac evaluation with biomarkers and echocardiography
Abdominal fat pad or bone marrow sampling as a lower-risk alternative to liver biopsy
Bone marrow examination to characterise the plasma cell clone
Cross-sectional imaging to document hepatomegaly and exclude focal lesions
redFlags: Rapidly progressive hepatomegaly with jaundice suggesting advanced infiltration
Signs of concurrent cardiac amyloid such as heart failure or arrhythmia, which dominate prognosis
Spontaneous bruising or bleeding indicating vascular fragility or acquired coagulation defects
Deep jaundice, which is associated with a poor short-term outcome
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is generally poor and is driven mainly by cardiac and renal involvement rather than by the liver; the appearance of significant jaundice signals advanced disease and short survival, although clone-directed therapy can improve outcomes in selected patients.
pitfalls: Attributing an isolated raised alkaline phosphatase and hepatomegaly to fatty liver without considering infiltration
Proceeding to percutaneous liver biopsy without recognising the elevated bleeding risk
Failing to type the amyloid, since management differs between AL, AA, and hereditary forms
Overlooking cardiac amyloid, which is the main determinant of survival
management: Clone-directed chemotherapy for the underlying AL amyloidosis, typically a bortezomib-based proteasome-inhibitor regimen combined with an anti-CD38 antibody such as daratumumab and a corticosteroid
Autologous haematopoietic stem cell transplantation in carefully selected patients with adequate organ reserve
For AA amyloid, suppression of the underlying chronic inflammatory disorder; for hereditary transthyretin disease, a TTR stabiliser or gene-silencing therapy

Supportive care of cholestasis and malnutrition with nutritional support and fat-soluble vitamin replacement, and correction of the amyloid-related bleeding tendency including acquired factor X deficiency
Baseline and serial assessment of cardiac and renal involvement that drive prognosis, alongside serum free light-chain monitoring to gauge haematological response
Careful management of hepatic decompensation and haemorrhage during acute deterioration, avoiding invasive procedures where perivascular deposition causes vascular fragility
Multidisciplinary care spanning haematology, hepatology and cardiology with referral to a specialist amyloidosis centre
Genetic counselling and family screening where a hereditary transthyretin form is identified
